title: Nehemiah 5:1–13
context: While the wall is being rebuilt, a crisis breaks out inside the community. Poorer Jews cry out that famine, the king's tribute, and debt have forced them to mortgage their land and even sell their children into bondage to fellow Jews. Nehemiah is angry, confronts the nobles and rulers for exacting usury from their brothers, and calls a great assembly. He points to his own lending and asks them to stop and restore what they have taken. They agree, take an oath before the priests, and the assembly says "Amen" and praises the LORD.

verses.text: Then there arose a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brothers the Jews.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then there arose a great cry of the people and of their wives against their brothers the Jews.” Arminian readers note that the threat now comes from within, as some in the community choose to profit from others' hardship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the outcry comes while the wall is still being built (5:16). Opposition from outside (chapter 4) is followed by injustice within, which can do as much harm to God's work.

verses.text: For there were some who said, “We, our sons and our daughters, are many. Let us get grain, that we may eat and live.”
verses.arminianNotes: Some say their families are large and they need grain "that we may eat and live." Arminian readers note the plain human need behind the outcry, as families struggle simply to survive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the first complaint is about food for many children. God's law called his people to uphold a poor brother "that your brother may live among you" (Leviticus 25:35–36).

verses.text: There were also some who said, “We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses. Let us get grain, because of the famine.”
verses.arminianNotes: Others are mortgaging fields, vineyards, and houses "because of the famine." Arminian readers see families forced into hard choices by circumstances outside their control.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that famine turns ordinary hardship into a crisis that exposes the community's character. The question is whether those with means will help or take advantage.

verses.text: There were also some who said, “We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute using our fields and our vineyards as collateral.
verses.arminianNotes: Others have borrowed against their fields and vineyards to pay the king's tribute. Arminian readers note that imperial taxation adds a burden the poor cannot carry alone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people live under Persian rule and its demands. Outside pressure is real, but the chapter's focus will be on how fellow Jews respond to it.

verses.text: Yet now our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers, our children as their children. Behold, we bring our sons and our daughters into bondage to be servants, and some of our daughters have been brought into bondage. It is also not in our power to help it, because other men have our fields and our vineyards.”
verses.arminianNotes: "Our flesh is as the flesh of our brothers" yet their children are going into bondage. Arminian readers see a moving appeal to shared kinship and the pain of families who cannot protect their own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the appeal rests on the people's common identity before God. Second Kings 4:1 shows a creditor taking children as slaves, a hardship God's people were not to inflict on one another.

verses.text: I was very angry when I heard their cry and these words.
verses.arminianNotes: “I was very angry when I heard their cry and these words.” Arminian readers see righteous anger at injustice, an emotion that moves Nehemiah to act on behalf of the oppressed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah's anger is directed at wrongdoing against God's people. Anger rightly aimed at injustice reflects God's own concern for the poor.

verses.text: Then I consulted with myself, and contended with the nobles and the rulers, and said to them, “You exact usury, everyone of his brother.” I held a great assembly against them.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah "consulted with myself," then contends with the nobles: "You exact usury, everyone of his brother." Arminian readers note his self-control, pausing to think before he acts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the law forbade interest from a poor brother (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19). Nehemiah confronts the leaders publicly by calling a great assembly.

verses.text: I said to them, “We, after our ability, have redeemed our brothers the Jews that were sold to the nations; and would you even sell your brothers, and should they be sold to us?” Then they held their peace, and found not a word to say.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah reminds them, “We, after our ability, have redeemed our brothers the Jews that were sold to the nations; and would you even sell your brothers, and should they be sold to us?” They find nothing to say. Arminian readers see the leaders confronted with the contradiction of their conduct.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the silence of the nobles concedes the charge. Nehemiah's argument exposes the absurdity of redeeming brothers from foreigners only to enslave them again at home.

verses.text: Also I said, “The thing that you do is not good. Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the nations, our enemies?
verses.arminianNotes: “Shouldn’t you walk in the fear of our God because of the reproach of the nations, our enemies?” Arminian readers note that the people's conduct either honors God or brings reproach before watching neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the fear of God is the root of right dealing with others. Leviticus 25:36 joins the two: "Take no interest from him or profit; but fear your God."

verses.text: I likewise, my brothers and my servants, lend them money and grain. Please let us stop this usury.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah says he and his household also lend money and grain: "Please let us stop this usury." Arminian readers note that he includes himself, appealing as one who shares responsibility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the humility of Nehemiah’s appeal in the words “Please let us stop this usury.” He leads by example and does not place himself above the reform he is asking of others.

verses.text: Please restore to them, even today, their fields, their vineyards, their olive groves, and their houses, also the hundredth part of the money, and of the grain, the new wine, and the oil, that you are charging them.”
verses.arminianNotes: He asks them to restore fields, vineyards, olive groves, houses, and "the hundredth part" they are charging. Arminian readers see repentance made concrete in restitution, not just in words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reform requires returning what was taken, even today. True repentance repairs harm done to others where it can.

verses.text: Then they said, “We will restore them, and will require nothing of them. We will do so, even as you say.” Then I called the priests, and took an oath of them, that they would do according to this promise.
verses.arminianNotes: They promise to restore and require nothing, and Nehemiah has them take an oath before the priests. Arminian readers note that the leaders freely commit themselves, and the oath binds them publicly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Nehemiah secures the promise with an oath before God's priests. A solemn commitment helps guard against the reform being quietly abandoned later.

verses.text: Also I shook out my lap, and said, “So may God shake out every man from his house, and from his labor, that doesn’t perform this promise; even may he be shaken out and emptied like this.” All the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised the LORD. The people did according to this promise.
verses.arminianNotes: Nehemiah shakes out his lap: "So may God shake out every man" who breaks the promise. The assembly says "Amen" and praises the LORD. Arminian readers see a community choosing obedience together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the symbolic act places the promise under God’s judgment. The chapter’s reform ends in worship, as all the assembly praises the LORD and does what was promised.
